{{Short description|Christmas carol and Marian hymn of German origin}} {{Use dmy dates|date=December 2024}} {{Infobox musical composition | name = {{Lang|de|Es ist ein Ros entsprungen||italic=no}} | type = [[Christmas carol]] | image = Speyerer Gesangbuch Es ist ein Ros entsprungen.jpg | alt = | caption = First printed in the 1599 ''Speyer Hymnal'' | translation = {{Bulleted list|Lo, how a rose e'er blooming|A Spotless Rose|Behold a Rose of Judah}} | genre = [[Hymn]] | occasion = [[Christmas]] | language = German | written = before the 17th century | based_on = | misc = }} "'''{{Lang|de|Es ist ein Ros entsprungen|italic=no}}'''" ({{Literal translation|A rose has sprung up}}) is a [[Christmas carol]] and [[Hymns to Mary|Marian hymn]] of German origin. It is most commonly translated into English as "'''Lo, how a rose e'er blooming'''" and is also called "'''A Spotless Rose'''" and "'''Behold a Rose of Judah'''". The [[rose symbolism|rose]] in the German text is a symbolic reference to the [[Virgin Mary]]. The hymn makes reference to the [[Old Testament prophecies]] of [[Book of Isaiah|Isaiah]], which in Christian interpretation foretell the [[Incarnation (Christianity)|Incarnation of Jesus]], and to the [[Tree of Jesse]], a traditional symbol of the [[Genealogy of Jesus|lineage of Jesus]]. Because of its prophetic theme, the hymn is popular during the Christian season of [[Advent]]. The hymn has its roots in an unknown author before the 17th century. It first appeared in print in 1599 in [[Cologne]] and has since been published with a varying number of verses and in several translations. It is most commonly sung to a melody harmonized by the German composer [[Michael Praetorius]] in 1609. The hymn's popularity endures in the 20th and 21st centuries.{{Cite magazine|url=https://www.theatlantic.com/entertainment/archive/2015/12/lo-how-a-rose-eer-blooming/421518/|title='Lo, How a Rose E'er Blooming' Is a Musician's Christmas Carol|first=Robinson|last=Meyer|date=25 December 2015|magazine=[[The Atlantic]]}} ==Meaning== [[File:St.Lambrecht Stammbaum Jesu.jpg|thumb|The hymn evokes the [[Rose (symbolism)|symbolic use of the rose]] to describe Mary sprouting from the [[Tree of Jesse]] as the [[Mother of God]] (altarpiece, [[Saint Lambert's Abbey]])]] The hymn was originally written with two verses that describe the fulfillment of the prophecy of [[Isaiah]] foretelling the [[Nativity of Jesus|birth of Jesus]]. It emphasizes the royal [[genealogy of Jesus]] and [[Christian messianic prophecies]]. The hymn describes a rose sprouting from the stem of the [[Tree of Jesse]], a symbolic device that depicts the descent of Jesus from [[Jesse (biblical figure)|Jesse]] of [[Bethlehem]], the father of King [[David]].{{cite book|last1=Pfatteicher|first1=Philip H.|title=Journey into the Heart of God: Living the Liturgical Year|date=2013|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=9780199997145|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=hfVdAAAAQBAJ&q=Es%20ist%20ein%20Ros%20entsprungen%20advent&pg=PP83|access-date=29 November 2017|language=en|chapter=2. Advent}} The image was especially popular in medieval times, and it features in many works of religious art from the period. It has its origin in the Book of Isaiah: {{blockquote|text=And there shall come forth a rod out of the stem of Jesse, and a Branch shall grow out of his roots.|source={{Bibleverse|Isaiah|11:1|KJV}}}} The second verse of the hymn, written in the first person, then explains to the listener the meaning of this symbolism: That Mary, the mother of Jesus, is the rose that has sprung up to bring forth the Christ child, represented as a small flower ''("das Blümlein")''. The German text affirms that Mary is a "pure maiden" ''("die reine Magd")'', emphasizing the doctrine of the [[Virgin birth of Jesus]].{{citation needed|date=December 2020}} In Theodore Baker's 1894 English translation, on the other hand, the second verse indicates that the rose symbolizes the infant Christ.{{Cite book|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=RUXNDwAAQBAJ&q=%22lo%2C+how+a+rose%22+refers+Jesus&pg=PT117|title=Hosanna in Excelsis: Hymns and Devotions for the Christmas Season|first1=David|last1=Leeman|first2=Barbara|last2=Leeman|date=6 October 2020|publisher=Moody Publishers|isbn=9780802498854}} Since the 19th century, other verses have been added, both in German and in translation.{{citation needed|date=December 2020}} ==History== [[File:Es ist ein Ros entsprungen, Wissenschaftliche Bibliothek Trier, Hs 2363 2304 (fol. 169r).jpg|thumb|Oldest known version of the hymn, manuscript 2363/2304 8° in the Trier City Library]] The poetry of Isaiah's prophecy has featured in Christian hymns since at least the 8th century, when [[Cosmas of Maiuma|Cosmas the Melodist]] wrote a hymn about the Virgin Mary flowering from the Root of Jesse, "{{lang|grc|Ῥάβδος ἐκ τῆς ῥίζης|italic=no}}", translated in 1862 by [[John Mason Neale]] as "Rod of the Root of Jesse".{{cite book|title=Hymns of the Eastern Church|author=John Mason Neale|author-link=John Mason Neale|publisher=Christian Classic Ethereal Library|page=77|citeseerx=10.1.1.693.1215}} The text of "{{Lang|de|Es ist ein Ros entsprungen|italic=no}}" dates from the 15th century. Its author is unknown. Its earliest source is in a manuscript from the [[Carthusian]] {{ill|Monastery of St Alban|de|Kloster Karthaus (Konz)}}, in [[Trier]], Germany, that is now preserved in the {{ill|Trier City Library|de|Stadtbibliothek Trier (Weberbach)}} and is thought to have been in use at the time of [[Martin Luther]]. The hymn first appeared in print in the late 16th century in the ''{{ill|Speyer Hymnbook|de|Alte Catholische Geistliche Kirchengeseng auff die fürnemste Feste}}'' (1599).{{cite book|last1=Roth|first1=Nancy|title=Praise, My Soul: Meditating on Hymns|date=2001|publisher=Church Publishing, Inc.|isbn=9780898693744|page=11|chapter-url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZTJEAwAAQBAJ&q=Friedrich%20Layriz%20es%20ist%20ein%20ros%20entsprungen&pg=PA11|access-date=29 November 2017|language=en|chapter=Hymn 81: Lo How a Rose e'er blooming}} The hymn has been used by both [[Catholics]] and [[Protestants]], with the focus of the song being [[Mary (mother of Jesus)|Mary]] or [[Jesus]], respectively.{{cite web|url=http://www.hymnsandcarolsofchristmas.com/Hymns_and_Carols/Notes_On_Carols/lo_how_a_rose_eer_blooming.htm|title=Lo How A Rose Eer Blooming – Notes|work=hymnsandcarolsofchristmas.com|access-date=18 December 2016}} In addition, there have been numerous versions of the hymn, with varying texts and lengths. In 1844, the German [[Hymnology|hymnologist]] {{ill|Friedrich Layriz|de}} added three more stanzas,{{cite book |last1=Herbst |first1=Wolfgang |title=Wer ist wer im Gesangbuch? |year=2001 |publisher=Vandenhoeck & Ruprecht |isbn=978-3-525-50323-2 |page=193 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=b_aO9wVNulYC |access-date=17 December 2020 |language=de}}{{cite web |last1=Publishing |first1=Alojado |title=Lied Es ist ein Ros' entsprungen |url=https://www.lieder-archiv.de/es_ist_ein_ros_entsprungen-notenblatt_200034.html |website=lieder-archiv.de |access-date=17 December 2020 |language=de}} the first of which, "{{Lang|de|Das Blümelein so kleine|italic=no}}", remained popular and has been included in Catholic{{cite web|url=http://gotteslob.katholisch.de/index.php?name=Suchbegriff&sbid=&thema=&source=new&pageid=18|title=Gotteslob Online|website=gotteslob.katholisch.de|access-date=18 December 2016}} and Protestant hymnals.[[Evangelisches Gesangbuch]], no. 30, and ''Gesangbuch der Evangelisch-reformierten Kirchen der deutschsprachigen Schweiz'' ([[Swiss Reformed Church]] hymnal), no. 399 The tune generally used for the hymn originally appeared in the ''[[Speyer]] Hymnal'' (printed in Cologne in 1599), and the familiar harmonization was written by German composer [[Michael Praetorius]] in 1609. A [[Canon (music)|canon]] version for four voices also exists, based on Praetorius's harmony and sometimes attributed to his contemporary, [[Melchior Vulpius]].{{cite web|title=Stile Antico|url=http://www.chambermusic.org/uploads/6/5/1/0/6510495/sa.pdf|website=The Friends of Chamber Music|publisher=the friends of chamber music endowment early music series|access-date=25 November 2017|archive-date=1 December 2017|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20171201040242/http://www.chambermusic.org/uploads/6/5/1/0/6510495/sa.pdf|url-status=dead}} The [[Metre (hymn)|metre]] of the hymn is 76.76.676. {{Listen|type=music|image=none|help=no|filename=Es ist ein Ros entsprungen (Prätorius).mid|title=Praetorius harmonization|filename2=U.S. Army Band - Lo How a Rose.ogg|title2=Lo, How a Rose E'er Blooming|description2=Performed by the chorus of the U.S. Army Band, c. 2010}} In 1896, [[Johannes Brahms]] used the hymn's tune as the base for a [[chorale prelude]] for organ, one of his ''[[Eleven Chorale Preludes]]'' Op. 122, later transcribed for orchestra by [[Erich Leinsdorf]].{{IMSLP|work=11 Chorale Preludes, Op.122 (Brahms, Johannes)|cname=''11 Chorale Preludes'', Op. 122 (Brahms)}}{{cite book|last1=Owen|first1=Barbara|title=The Organ Music of Johannes Brahms|date=2007|publisher=Oxford University Press, USA|isbn=9780195311075|page=104|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=Qn88DwAAQBAJ&q=brahms%20chorale%20prelude%20es%20ist%20ein%20ros&pg=PA104|access-date=25 November 2017}}{{cite book|last=Bloom|first=Julius|title=The Year in American Music: 1946–1947|year=1946|page=497|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7_E5AAAAIAAJ|access-date=25 November 2017|publisher=Allen, Towne & Heath}} During the [[Nazi era]], many German Christmas carols were rewritten to promote [[Nazism|National Socialist ideology]] and to excise references to the Jewish origins of Jesus. During [[Christmas in Nazi Germany]], "{{Lang|de|Es ist ein Ros entsprungen|italic=no}}" was rewritten as "{{Lang|de|Uns ist ein Licht erstanden / in einer dunklen Winternacht|italic=no}}" ("A light has arisen for us / on a dark winter night"), with a secularised text evoking sunlight falling on the [[Fatherland]] and extolling the virtues of motherhood.{{cite news|last1=Schwind|first1=Elisabeth|title=Lieb aus deinem göttlichen Mund|url=https://www.suedkurier.de/nachrichten/kultur/Lieb-aus-deinem-goettlichen-Mund;art10399,9059751|access-date=29 November 2017|work=[[Südkurier]]|date=23 December 2016|language=de}} The hymn's melody has been used by a number of composers, including [[Hugo Distler]] who used it as the base for his 1933 [[oratorio]] {{Lang|de|Die Weihnachtsgeschichte}} (The Christmas Story).{{cite book|last1=Liebergen|first1=Patrick M.|title=Singer's Library of Song: A Vocal Anthology of Masterworks and Folk Songs From the Medieval Era Through the Twentieth Century : Book Medium|date=2005|publisher=Alfred Music Publishing|isbn=9780739036600|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=he0YWp2oO4QC&q=es%20ist%20ein%20ros%20Hugo%20Distler&pg=PA122|access-date=25 November 2017}} [[Arnold Schoenberg]]'s ''Weihnachtsmusik'' (1921) for two violins, cello, piano and harmonium is a short fantasy on ''Es ist ein Ros entsprungen'' with ''[[Stille Nacht]]'' as a [[counterpoint|contrapuntal]] melody.{{cite book|last=MacDonald|first=Malcolm|author-link=Malcolm MacDonald (music critic)|title=Schoenberg|date=2008|publisher=Oxford University Press|isbn=9780198038405|page=266|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=VsaFwzCMNa4C&q=Schoenberg%20Weihnachtsmusik&pg=PA266|access-date=25 November 2017}} In 1990, [[Jan Sandström (composer)|Jan Sandström]] wrote {{Lang|de|[[Es ist ein Ros entsprungen (Sandström)|Es ist ein Ros entsprungen]]}} for two [[a cappella]] choirs, which incorporates the setting of Praetorius in choir one. ===English translations=== Well-known versions of the hymn have been published in various English translations. [[Theodore Baker]]'s "Lo, How a Rose E'er Blooming" was written in 1894 and appears in the [[Psalter Hymnal]] ([[Christian Reformed Church in North America]]) and [[The United Methodist Hymnal]] (American [[United Methodist Church]]).{{cite web|url=http://www.hymnary.org/hymn/PsH/351|title=Psalter Hymnal (Gray) 351. Lo, how a rose e'er blooming|work=hymnary.org|access-date=18 December 2016}}{{cite web |title="Es ist ein Ros entsprungen" – A German Christmas Carol in German and English |url=https://www.german-way.com/history-and-culture/german-language/german-christmas-carols/es-ist-ein-ros-entsprungen-lo-how-a-rose-eer-blooming/ |website=german-way.com |access-date=18 December 2020}} The British hymn translator [[Catherine Winkworth]] translated the first two verses of the hymn as "A Spotless Rose".{{cite book|last=Winkworth|first=Catherine|author-link=Catherine Winkworth|title=Christian Singers of Germany|year=1869|publisher=Macmillan|isbn=978-0-598-64823-5|page=85|url=https://books.google.com/books?id=ZDoCAAAAQAAJ&dq=winkworth+es+ist+ein+ros&pg=PP16|access-date=18 December 2020}} In 1919 the British composer [[Herbert Howells]] set this text as a [[motet]] for [[SATB]] choir. Howells stated that:
I sat down and wrote A Spotless Rose...after idly watching some shunting from the window of a cottage in Gloucester which overlooked the [[Midland Railway]]. In an upstairs room I looked out on iron railings and the main [[Bristol and Gloucester Railway|Bristol to Gloucester railway]] line, with shunting trucks bumping and banging. I wrote it and dedicated to my mother – it always moves me when I hear it, just as if it were written by someone else.{{cite book|last=Palmer|first=Christopher|title=Herbert Howells: a study|year=1978|page=16}}
Howells' carol is [[through-composed]], switching between {{music|time|7|8}}, {{music|time|5|4}} and {{music|time|5|8}} time signatures, unconventional for a carol of this era.{{cite web|author=Phillip Cooke|title=On Herbert Howells's 'A Spotless Rose'...|url=https://www.phillipcooke.com/blog/on-herbert-howellss-a-spotless-rose|website=phillipcooke.com|access-date=12 December 2020}} The plangent final [[cadence]] ("On a cold, cold winter's night"), with its multiple [[Suspension (music)|suspension]]s is particularly celebrated. Howells' contemporary, [[Patrick Hadley]] reportedly told the composer "I should like, when my time comes, to pass away with that magical cadence".{{cite book|last=Spicer|first=Paul|author-link=Paul Spicer (musician)|title=Herbert Howells|date=1998|page=67}} Winkworth's translation was again set to music in 2002 by the British composer and academic Sir [[Philip Ledger]].{{cite web|url=http://www.sirphilipledger.com/ledger.php?section=pub|title=Sir Philip Ledger|work=sirphilipledger.com|access-date=18 December 2016|archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20110414010013/http://www.sirphilipledger.com/ledger.php?section=pub|archive-date=14 April 2011|url-status=dead}} A further English translation of the hymn, "Behold, a rose is growing", was written by the American Lutheran musician and writer, [[Harriet Reynolds Krauth Spaeth]] (1845–1925). Her four-verse version is often published with an additional 5th verse, translated by the American theologian John Caspar Mattes (1876–1948).{{cite web |title=Behold, a Branch is Growing |url=https://hymnary.org/text/behold_a_branch_is_growing |website=Hymnary.org |access-date=28 December 2020}}{{cite book |title=Evangelical Lutheran Hymnary |date=May 1996 |publisher=Morning Star Music Publishers/Evangelical Lutheran Church/Evangelical Lutheran Synod Worship Committee |isbn=978-0-944529-18-8 |page=121 |url=https://books.google.com/books?id=7qCqPQAACAAJ}} Another Christmas hymn, "A Great and Mighty Wonder", is set to the same tune as this carol and may sometimes be confused with it. It is, however, a hymn by [[Germanus of Auxerre]], "{{lang|grc|Μέγα καὶ παράδοξον θαῦμα|italics=no}}", translated from Greek to English by [[John Mason Neale]] in 1862. Versions of the German lyrics have been mixed with Neale's translation of a Greek hymn in subsequent versions such as [[Percy Dearmer]]'s version in the 1931 ''[[Songs of Praise (hymnal)|Songs of Praise]]'' collection and ''[[Carols for Choirs]]'' (1961).{{cite web|url=http://carols.co/a-great-and-mighty-wonder/ |title=A Great and Mighty Wonder |access-date=2011-12-09 |url-status=dead |archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20120425024609/http://carols.co/a-great-and-mighty-wonder/ |archive-date=25 April 2012 }} ==Lyrics== {| class="wikitable" |- ! scope="col" | German original ! scope="col" | Baker's version ! scope="col" | Winkworth's version ! scope="col" | Spaeth's translation
